title: Hebbian learning: cells that fire together wire together
idea: When one brain cell keeps helping another to fire, the link between them grows stronger. Learning, in this view, is the slow strengthening of connections that get used together.

cameFrom.label: Neuroscience and psychology
cameFrom.note: Hebb had worked with the surgeon Wilder Penfield on patients after brain operations and with Karl Lashley on vision in rats, and wanted a theory that linked behaviour to brain cells.

people.note: Canadian psychologist at McGill University in Montreal who tied learning and memory to the way brain cells are wired together.

papers.title: The Organization of Behavior: A Neuropsychological Theory
papers.publisher: John Wiley & Sons, New York (book; reissued by Psychology Press)
papers.summary: The book proposed that cells which repeatedly fire together become linked into cell assemblies that hold a memory or an idea. Its learning rule, stated in words rather than equations, became the template for adjusting connection strengths in artificial networks.

steps.heading: Two cells and a link
steps.body: Cell A sends signals to cell B through a connection, and the connection has a strength.

steps.heading: Use strengthens the link
steps.body: When A is active and takes part in making B fire, the strength of the connection from A to B grows.

steps.heading: Written as a formula
steps.body: Later researchers wrote the rule as: change in strength = learning rate × activity of A × activity of B. Hebb himself gave no formula.

steps.heading: Cell assemblies
steps.body: Groups of cells that keep firing together become wired into an assembly. Switching on part of the assembly can switch on the rest, which is how a whole memory could come back from a fragment.

steps.heading: The catch
steps.body: Strengthening alone only ever grows, so connection strengths run away unless something holds them back. Later learning rules added decay or normalisation.

steps.heading: The slogan came later
steps.body: The phrase "cells that fire together wire together" is a later summary, usually credited to the neuroscientist Carla Shatz in 1992. Hebb's own wording is longer and more careful about timing: A must help to cause B's firing.
